EDITORIAL 


ON 

Choosing 
a Camp 


It won’t be very long now before 
parents of camp age youngsters may 
be faced with the problem of choosing 
a camp to which little Johnny or little 
Mary may be directed this summer. 
For some parents, of course, the prob¬ 
lem is easy. They know just the camp. 
Either big brother or big sister has 
been there in former years; or the 
lady next door sends her youngsters 
to Camp Fiddle Faddle, and they have 
had such a nice time; or an enterpris¬ 
ing camp promotion scheme has raised 
the question. Whatever the reason, the 
problem has been quickly solved in 
such instances. 

There will be alway * the year of new 
adventure when the choosing of a 
camp will be a brand new experience 
for parents and for the boys or girls 
fortunate*enough to be on the receiving 
end of a camp holiday. And so this 
message is addressed to parents of new 
campers in 1958. How are you going 
to choose a camp? 

It should be obvious that whatever 
camping experience the potential 
camper is to have should be valuable 
to him. Do you know your boy or 
girl well enough, parents, to say what 
is best for him or her insofar as camp 
interests are concerned? Or are you 
aware of the significant traits of per¬ 
sonality? Or the capacity he has to do 
the kinds of things children can do at 
camp? Do you know your own child? 

Parents should acquaint themselves 
with those people who will be respon- 


By Hart. M. Devenney , M.A. 

sible for their children at camp. Do 
you know the director? Do you know 
his point of view in regard to camping 
. . . how he feels about children? What 
are the aims of his camp? What prac¬ 
tices are followed? What about the 
training and experience of the director, 
of the staff? Are the counsellors 
emotionally mature? Are they trained 
and experienced in the job of being 
counsellors? Do you feel that they are 
truly interested in camping? 

Then too, parents, it is very impor¬ 
tant that you know something about 
the kind of programme opportunities 
to be offered your child. For remember, 
these will be media through which 
your child will add to his learning. 
Does the programme of the camp you 
are considering meet the needs and 
interests of your boy or girl? It is 
suggested that camps can provide op¬ 
portunities for the development of 
independence; they can provide oppor¬ 
tunities for developing the ability to 
get along with others; they can enable 
campers to understand groups and 
other individuals of varied back¬ 
grounds. 

It should go without saying that 
camps should contribute to the im¬ 
provement of health, to the advance¬ 
ment of certain skills and, of course, 
to the appreciation of outdoor interests. 
All this can be done through partici¬ 
pation in programme. As a further 
check, note the kind of site, facilities 
and equipment available because there 
is a definite relationship between these 
and the ability to fulfill the programme 

continued on page 210 


Toronto , Canada , June 1958

NATURAL 
SCIENCE 
AT CAMP 


By F. A. Urquhart, M.A ., Ph.D 

Head of the Division of Zoology and 
Palaeontology , Royal Ontario Museum , 
Toronto. 


Prepared from an address given 
at the joint conference of the 
Canadian and Quebec Camping 
Associations held in Montreal on 
April 12 th, 1958. 


During the past twenty-three years 
I have had the real pleasure of taking 
part, directly or indirectly, in the pre¬ 
sentation of various aspects of Natural 
Science in summer camps. May I at 
the outset, state most emphatically 
that one serious fault common to many 
camps is that those in charge of Na¬ 
tural Science try to accomplish far too 
much in too short a period of time. A 
camp should be a place of pleasure in 
the out-of-doors. It should not be an 
outdoor classroom. It is impossible to 
do more than introduce the camper to 
some aspects of Natural Science in the 
short period of four to six weeks, and 
in periods of one to two weeks only a 
very general consideration of Natural 
Science as a whole can be presented. 
Secondly, I would emphasize that the 
amateur is in a far better position to 
present an interesting and challenging 
programme to children than is the 
professional naturalist or the too well- 
informed naturalist. An amateur’s in¬ 
terest is a lively one, full of ideas and 
sparkling with initiative. This feeling 


of venturing into a new and exciting 
field rubs off on the children and 
stimulates their interest. I therefore 
direct remarks to you who are en¬ 
thusiastic amateur counsellors and 
directors. 

I will deal briefly with the four 
major aspects of Natural Science: the 
sky (astronomy); the atmosphere (me¬ 
teorology); the earth (geology and 
mineralogy); life (botany and zoology). 

One of my most vivid recollections 
concerns taking part in a “sky-gazing” 
episode at one of the camps. It con¬ 
sisted in lying in a comfortable position 
on your back so that your gaze was 
directed skyward. The counsellor, a 
most capable young lady, proceeded 
to discuss with the group the immensity 
of our universe, pointing out some of 
the more obvious stars and star clus¬ 
ters. She did not expect us to memorize 
the names and positions of the various 
constellations, which would have dulled 
rather than whetted our appetites for 
further knowledge. She knew that 
books were available and the sky was 
omnipresent. She brought the science 
close to earth by demonstrating how to 
use the north star to find your approxi¬ 
mate latitude. The talk was simple. 
The results magnificent. A challenging 
programme. 


170 


Canadian Camping 






Terms such as fronts, air masses and 
pressure areas are fairly common 
knowledge. Most adults, and many 
children, are cognizant of the inter¬ 
action of air masses in the production 
of weather. A consideration of factors 
involved in weather fits in very well 
with tripping. Before the counsellors 
start out on their proposed canoe or 
hiking trip, a brief consideration of the 
weather to be expected makes the sub¬ 
ject a part of the adventure. This 
briefing is given by the Natural Science 
Counsellor, and is concerned with wind 
direction, cloud types and pressure 
changes — an aneroid barometer, like 
a• compass, should be permanent equip¬ 
ment in every camp. As these various 
items of weather are encountered, they 
are reviewed by the counsellors in 
charge of the trips. 

The earth sciences are concerned 
with rocks, minerals and, of course, 
topography. A Natural Science Coun¬ 
sellor should be well informed about 
the topography of the country in which 
the camp is located, and should be 
able to explain briefly and clearly the 
factors involved in producing the vari¬ 
ous topographical aspects of the coun¬ 
tryside. A few of the common rocks 
and minerals might be identified, with 
particular reference to those that tell 
a story about the country as a whole 
— such as shales being formed by the 
deposition of mud in primordial seas, 
sandstones from sand, and granites 
from molten rock from the hot interior 
of the earth that poured out over the 
surface. In dealing with this subject, 
as in all others, care should be taken 
not to spoil the interest in the subject 
by involving the camper in too many 
details. I can recall one counsellor who, 
being too well versed in the subject of 
geology, killed the interest by dictating 
notes on igneous rocks under the sub¬ 
ject headings of the rhyolite-granite 
series, the trachyte-syenite series, the 


andesite-diorite series, and on and on, 
ad nauseum. 

Although a considerable amount of 
interest can be aroused in the camper 
on such subjects as astronomy, meteor- 
ology, geology and mineralogy, never¬ 
theless there is no subject of greater 
interest to the camper, particularly the 
young camper, than that of biology. 
The great delight in living out-of-doors 
is due to your physical proximity to 
live trees, live plants and animals. What 
camper has not felt a feeling of great 
joy, listening to the call of the loon on 
the shores of a pine-fringed northern 
lake! So great is the camper’s interest 
in the living natural sciences that he 
tries to digest everything, like a hungry 
boy at a birthday party. It is most es¬ 
sential that the camper be introduced 
to this fascinating world slowly, but 
with enthusiasm. As I have stated 
before, and it is worth repeating, an 
enthusiastic amateur is far superior to 
a well-informed professional naturalist 
or biologist. A good rule to follow, for 
camp directors, is to choose your nature 
counsellors for their enthusiasm rather 
than their knowledge. 

There are many species of plants in 
any given area. With very little effort, 
a professional botanist will collect 
many hundreds of different kinds of 
plants in a given geographic area. Some 
of these kinds of plants can be easily 
identified, while many of them are 
most difficult. I remember one coun¬ 
sellor who, wishing to be very scien¬ 
tific, referred to the various kinds of 
plants by their scientific names. On one 
trip the camper was introduced to such 
amazing plants as Taxacum officinale, 
Cirsium arvense, Comus canadensis, 
and others. Would it not have been 
better to name them dandelion, thistle, 
and bunchberry?. Indeed, it is better 
to refrain from identifying anything 
but the obvious and to collect for 


Toronto , Canada , June 1958 


171 



future reference only those which will 
stimulate the interest of the campers. 
And, while we are discussing the col¬ 
lecting of plants, I would point out 
that I have found the collecting of 
leaves of various species of deciduous 
trees most satisfactory in stimulating 
an interest in speciation and most re¬ 
warding in establishing a dynamic 
project. Most of our native Canadian 
trees are easy to identify (willows and 
hawthorns being exceptions). As a re¬ 
sult of such experience, I designed a 
leaf album for the beginner which 
simplifies the subject of preparing the 
specimen for the album and identify¬ 
ing them. Information concerning this 
leaf album may be obtained by writing 
to the University of Toronto Press. I 
am certain that you will find it most 
useful. 

Contrary to popular opinion, I do 
not feel that collecting specimens of 
animals is a good practice. In any one 
locality there are many thousands of 
different kinds of insects, and the ma¬ 
jority of them are most difficult to 
identify, and any attempt to do so leads 
only to frustration. To deal with insects 
as a- group, emphasizing their impor¬ 
tance in nature is, as a discussion, most 
rewarding. A particular butterfly or 
moth might be used as the basis of a 
discussion. A tree stump, the loose 
bark of dead trees, creeks, ponds and 
lakes should be examined for the pure 
enjoyment of discovering things and, 
having made the discovery, keep the 
interest alive by the use of group terms 
such as beetles, caterpillars, dragon¬ 
flies, mayflies, and so on. In brief, deal 
with insects to the order name only 
and leave the families, genera and 
species to the entomological enthusiast. 
Live amphibians (frogs, toads, sala¬ 
manders) and reptiles (snakes, turtles) 
can arouse much interest if brought 
into the camp and kept alive, in jars 
of sufficient size, for a few days. Care 


should be exercised, however, not to 
attempt keeping them too long. No 
sight is more disgusting than that of a 
bloated dead frog in a dirty jar. Bird 
watching is a pleasant pastime, and 
early morning trips can be most re¬ 
warding. Once again, however, one 
should not attempt to identify every 
warbler that is seen and every bird 
that is heard. I can well remember a 
particular camp that leaned heavily 
upon “bird watching” as a nature 
project. One student, after two weeks, 
was unable to identify the song of the 
white-throated sparrow, not because 
the song is so difficult to remember 
but there were too many songs of too 
many birds. A permanent camp should, 
of course, have available as many 
coloured illustrations of birds as pos¬ 
sible, in order to assist the camper to 
identify a particular bird that has been 
seen. 

Much could be written about nature 
projects in a camp. The success or 
failure of such a programme rests en¬ 
tirely upon the degree of imagination 
and ability of the counsellor involved. 
Every camp should, of course, have 
many reference books and a great 
many illustrations. Advice can be ob¬ 
tained from many sources. The division 
of Zoology and Palaeontology of the 
Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto 
has an exceptionally well-trained cura¬ 
torial staff that is always willing to 
answer your questions and to give you 
advice. The Canadian Audubon So¬ 
ciety in Toronto has a great deal of 
literature available and suggestions for 
many fine nature projects. 

In conclusion: whatever you do, 
keep the subject simple, and make your 
programme one that stimulates interest 
and imagination. If you do this, you 
will develop a challenging programme. 

—• 


172 


Canadian Camping 



SOME THOUGHTS 
ON 

CANOE TRIP CAMPINC 

By Douglas Lloyd , 

Canoeing Instructor and Director of 
Out-Trips, Camp Ahmek. 


Let us imagine that we are coun¬ 
sellors at a summer camp somewhere 
in the north woods, and that we are 
about to set out to learn more about 
Nature by taking a canoe-trip, in com¬ 
pany with a group of boys or girls. (A 
parallel can easily be made with a man 
and his family or friends.) What things 
should be done and when? 


CHECK LIST 
FOR COUNSELLORS 
PLANNING A CANOE TRIP 

A. Planning before involving campers. 

1. Do I know my group? 

(a) their interests? 

(b) their skills? 

(c) their physical capabilities? 

(d) their experience with outdoor 

living ? 

2. What routes are available? 

(a) Do I know any first-hand? 

(b) Consult your section director. 
(He should have suggestions.) 

(c) Consult your fellow 
counsellors. 

(d) Consult the tripping director. 


Note: — Do NOT expect the trip¬ 
ping director to plan your trip for you. 
He does not know your group or its 
capabilities. He can give you informa¬ 
tion pertinent to the timing, organiza¬ 
tion and difficulties of a particular 
route. The rest is up to you. 

B. Planning involving the campers. 

1. Have the campers been involved in 
the final selection of a route? 

2. Does the route selected suit them? 

(a) See A 1. 

(b) Are the campers intrigued by 
the things they will do and 
see on the trip? 

(c) Does the trip’s goal provide a 
climax which will satisfy them? 

(d) If the answer to any of ques¬ 
tions a, b or c is “no”, are you 
doing your best to resolve any 
difficulties ? 

3. Do you know what foods they like? 
(Menu-planning in detail is not 
within their scope, but they can 
make valuable suggestions.) 

4. Do they know where they are 
going, when they are leaving, when 
they are returning? Can they point 


Toronto , Canada , June 1958 


173 




out the route on a map ? Have they 
written home to tell their parents? 
Have you informed their parents 
of the exact details? 

5. Have you included one day of res* 
in four in your itinerary? Have you 
given thought to a programme for 
this rest day? (Suit the programme 
to area and interests, and vice- 
versa. ) 

6. Do your campers know what cloth¬ 
ing to take? Is it readily available? 
Check. 

7. Have you a first-hand knowledge of 
their camping skills? Try — 

(a) a meal out of camp; 

(b) a day out of camp; 

(c) an over-night. 

8. Do the campers know your 
staff-assistant? Do they have con¬ 
fidence in him? Do you? What 
have you done to involve him con¬ 
structively with the group? (Re¬ 
member that he must have enough 
prestige to carry on should anything 
happen to you.) 

C. Actual Preparation. 

1. Have you prepared in written form 
a day-by-day menu? 

2. Have you incorporated the foods 
your campers like? (see B 3.) 

3. Is the menu reasonably well- 
balanced ? 

4. Are you and the campers going to 
be able to carry the food you have 
ordered? Have too many canned 
goods been suggested? 

5. Have you included at least one 
evening meal which can be quickly 
and easily prepared? 

6. Did you make out your food order 
from this menu? 

7. Did you check off the food received 
on the food order? 

8. Did you list errors and omissions? 
A shortage of a major item can be 
serious. 


D. Packing. 

Note: let the campers pack accord¬ 
ing to their experience and age. 

1. The ideal is one pack per camper 
and one canoe per staff man for 
efficient travelling. 

2. Are you taking precautions to see 
that the packs are padded on the 
back, well-balanced, not round? 

3. Are the weights reasonable? 

(a) Assign a pack to each camper. 
Label it so it can be recognized. 

(b) Pre-test the camper’s ability to 
carry. 

(c) Take more packs if necessary. 
This is much better than hav¬ 
ing the campers unable to car¬ 
ry “their load” and save much 
heart-break and ill-temper. 

4. Are the packs reasonably water¬ 
tight ? 

5. Are the difficult articles carefully 
packed ? 

(i.e. Jam — inside billies.) 

6. Do you know where the axe, the 
first-aid kit, the utensils are? 

7. Has the food for the first lunch 
been set aside and packed where 
it can easily be obtained? (Sug¬ 
gestion — in pack with items listed 
in “6”.) 

8. Do the canoes balance? (slightly 
stern-heavy.) 

9. Does the load in the canoe, includ¬ 
ing passengers come under the 
maximum carrying capacity of the 
canoe in use? 

Note: points 1 to 9 apply on each 
successive day during trip.) 

E. On the way. 

1. Have you established an adequate 
routine for travel? 

(a) Does each camper know his 
responsibilities to the group? 

(b) Does each camper and staff- 
man know the safety rules? 


174 


Canadian Camping 



2. Are the campers constantly re¬ 
minded to note the “flora and 
fauna”? (If you show interest, so 
will they.) 

3. Have you a lunch campsite in 
mind? 

4. Have you an evening campsite in 
mind which can be reached by 3-4 
p.m. at the latest? An alternative? 

Notes: 

1. Have the courage and judgment to 
say “no” to the urge to shoot rapids 
or cross “white water”. When 
campers are involved, the answer 
is always “NO”. 

2. Watch for signs of fatigue. Take 
time out. The skill with which you 
do this is a measure of your leader¬ 
ship. 

F. On the campsite. 

1. How much daylight (or good 
weather) have you left? 

2. Are you looking after first things 
first? 

(a) Is the tent up? Ditches dug 
around it ? 

(b) Are the campers set for the 
night? (Check. Their judg¬ 
ment is poor.) 

(c) Have you an adequate supply 
of firewood for supper, evening 
programme AND breakfast. 
(To be able to leave enough 
good wood for the next trip 
is an indication of a well- 
planned trip which some day 
you in turn will appreciate.) 

(d) Have you checked the fire¬ 
place? Is it safe? 

3. Have you set aside the food for 
supper and evening programme? 


4. Have you stowed away all remain¬ 
ing supplies in a safe, dry place? 
(If you intend a very quick start 
the next morning, also set aside 
breakfast material. Prunes prepared 
the night before taste much better.) 

5. Is your mealtime routine set up 
and understood by all? (A revolv¬ 
ing routine in which all tasks, plea¬ 
sant and otherwise, are shared is 
well worth the initial trouble to 
set it up and saves tiresome orders 
and their resulting friction and un¬ 
fairness. ) 

6. Is the swimming area safe? Check 
it yourself and act as life-guard. 

7. Do you take the trouble to put on 
a pot for “hot-water and soap” 
dish-washing ? 

8. Have you a varied evening pro¬ 
gramme ? 

9. Are you able to break camp within 
an hour and a half of rising? 

10. Have you “drowned” your camp 
fire? (Inside and outside the fire¬ 
place. ) 

Note: “Early to bed and early to 

rise” was never truer than on a canoe 

trip. 

G. The Return. 

1. How is your morale? 

(a) Are the campers pulling to¬ 
gether ? 

(b) Can they enthuse over what 
they saw and did ? 

(c) Are they reasonably clean and 
tidy? Would you be proud to 
meet their parents on the dock 
or do you want to slink in the 
back door?

"WOODLORE" 


Art Address given at the Joint Con¬ 
ference of the Canadian and Quebec 
Camping Associations in Montreal, 
April 12, 1958. 

By PAUL PROVENCHER 

Timber Cruiser , Voyageur, 

Master Woodsman, Chief Forester , 

Author of 

11 1 Live in The Woods” 


More than anything else—the twang 
of a bow string—the flight of an arrow 
—or the dull impact of a stone arrow¬ 
head hitting a tree, are the things 
which have prompted many of our 
ancestors to learn in earnest the ways 
of the woods. 

Some found the new life very exact¬ 
ing and demanding, no doubt, while 
others accepted it with respect and 
made the best of it. Those who were 
born adventurers found it thrilling and 
fascinating, and Canada was there to 
give them their fuil share of adventure. 

My father did not help to intensify 
the urge I had for the great outdoors, 
because he is not a woodsman, he is a 
lawyer, and a good one at that, and 
I have a great deal of respect for him; 
but a lake is a lake to him and a 
mountain is a mountain. My grand¬ 
father was a good farmer, but he never 
developed a raste for trapping or fish¬ 
ing that I know ol. My great grand¬ 
father, I was told, was a good old 
genuine farmer. 

It comes from way back — nine 
generations back — Sebastien Proven- 
cher, known then as “Sebast”—was a 


rich man, the archives say . . . He 
landed here in 1663 and was the owner 
of a cow and servant! Times have 
changed; our dollar bill does not even 
have the shape of a beaver pelt now¬ 
adays, but there is something which 
has not changed so very much yet, and 
that is “Woodlore”. It is true that with 
the advent of helicopters, the ways of 
getting in or out of the woods have 
been simplified immensely, but “Wood- 
lore” becomes a “must” the moment 
you set foot outside of the cabin into 
the wilds of any country. 

How many Iroquois arrows flew over 
Sebast’s head before he realized that 
if he was to survive in this land of 
plenty, something had to be done — 
we will never know; but the fact is 
that farming in those conditions was 
done as a part-time job, and to exist, 
trapping was practiced to increase the 
meager revenue of the fields. Like 
many others, he took to the woods and 
became a “coureur-de-bois”. Eight 
years elapsed, when one day he was 
called by Intendant Talon to act as a 
guide on Father AlbanePs first trip to 
the Hudson Bay via Lake St. John. 
Unless the man had built up a reputa¬ 
tion as a “woodsman”, I doubt if he 
would have been picked up as one of 
the guides; and this leads us to the 
pertinent question of what is “wood- 
lore” and what are the fundamentals of 
it. 

In its widest acceptation, “woodlore” 
is the art to live off the land with only 
what nature has to offer. During the 
Stone Age, the articles used to hunt 
and to produce fire were very primitive 
indeed, and the caveman nevertheless 
did survive. When the American Indi¬ 
ans set foot on this continent, although 
there had been some evolution in the 
shape of the weapons used for killing 
animals, the bow and arrow and the 
making of fire by friction were still the 
only means of producing what is neces¬ 
sary to maintain life. 


176 


Canadian Camptng 



For a city man in 1958, “Woodlore” 
is a word which is mentioned only 
occasionally, and we see it in the daily 
papers only when some inexperienced 
hunter gets lost and dies from exposure 
in the woods. 

For the Indian born in a Montagnais 
wigwam on a mattress of balsam 
boughs, hundreds of miles from civili¬ 
zation, where his first contact with the 
world is the sting of wood smoke 
through the delicate tissue of his lungs, 
“Woodlore” more or less grows with 
him and it becomes second nature; but 
for us — the famous art to live off the 
land is a challenge. 

Nature is a good provider, but unless 
we go back to the past and practice or 
at least understand what to do to find 
our way back to safety, and to provide 
food and heat, we had better stay put 
where we are, amid streetcars, concrete 
sidewalks and subways. 

Our Indians had fire at their disposal 
and the bow and arrow to provide 
their families with food and a relative 
comfort. It was not easy, and they had 
to be good at calling animals to them 
in those days, because the bow was only 
efficient at 75 feet. Many a time food 
was scarce and Champlain himself wit¬ 
nessed the throwing of live animals into 
a messy soup of boiling intestines and 
stomachs of other beasts to appease the 
pangs of hunger of famished hunters. 
Traps, deadfalls of all kinds were in¬ 
vented by the observant hunters, and 
the more cunning and expert they be¬ 
came, the more pleasure they derived 
from a life which to us would be 
unbearable and disastrous. Above all, 
these men were self-confident for one 
good reason, because they knew where 
they were at all times in the forests. 
They did not have the compass to help 
them, but they knew of the march of 
the sun and they had observed that 
Polaris was the only star above their 


heads which did not travel in space. 
The winds when set in one direction, 
in different regions, stayed set for a 
period of time. Today, these things 
have not changed and for any camper 
they must be known because they are 
the fundamentals of “woodlore”. 

We are fortunate indeed, to have at 
our disposal the most accurate maps 
of the land and the best of compasses. 
My first advice to “Commandoes” on 
my survival course was that they keep 
an extra map of the country in the 
lining of their battle-dress, and to be¬ 
come experts in reading the compass. 
Foggy weather fools even the experts, 
and only the combination of a map 
and compass and their understanding 
will take a camper back to safety. The 
Indian relied on the sun and sometimes 
the wind, to find his directions — why 
should we not do the same? This is 
okay you would think, but what about 
rainy and foggy weather? The Indian 
does not travel in rainy and foggy 
weather, he knows how to live, why 
should we get wet ourselves and take a 
chance to get lost? Again, your ques¬ 
tion would be, “Yes, but we have a 
map and compass and we know how 
to use it”. Then, I may ask, what if 
there is mineral in the soil and the 
needle of your compass gets “crazy”? 
... If, even in good sunny weather 
you want to travel more accurately, 
then orient yourself often during your 
travels. 

1. Lay the map flat on the ground, 
then place the center of your com¬ 
pass approximately over the point 
where you stand; let the needle 
settle; you then will note that it 
will always point to the North. 

2. Rotate the map underneath until 
the magnetic north of the map be¬ 
comes parallel to your compass 
needle. 


Toronto , Canada , June 1958 


177 



3. Then with the complete lay-out of 
the country on your map and be¬ 
fore your eyes, decide on which lake 
you want to go. 

4. Look at the bearing and take a 
note of it. 

5. Observe where the rays of the sun 
strike your body, and look at the 
surrounding country for landmarks. 

6. Fold your map and make the needle 
read the noted bearing. 

7. Sight on a landmark, go there, and 
take another reading — it is that 
simple and that easy. Before you 
leave to proceed along to the next 
landmark, check yourself on the 
sun, it will give you more con¬ 
fidence. 

To provide food: axe, fishhooks, 
lines, snare wire, a small steel trap 
and a fish net are important things 
to put into your packsack. They take 
little space and are so light to carry. 
For fire, I always carry one of those 
waterproof safety boxes folding 20 or 
so matches. When I asked one day an 
elderly Naskaupee trapper at Fort 
MacKenzie, if they used the kind of 
oil-tanned thong I carried about my 
belt to make fire by friction, they all 
looked at me as if I was a “greenhorn” 
and they started to laugh heartily. 
“Naskaupee Indians never run short 
of matches”, he said. 

I know of an old trapper who had 
to carry his own fire for at least one 
week on his toboggan to reach a cabin, 
where he knew there were matches. 
Fire by friction is a tedious job and 
unless obliged to do so, stick to 
matches. Fire can be made by firing a 
shotgun shell in which you have re¬ 
placed the lead pellets by dry wads of 
rags or paper. 

“Woodlore” means also a certain 
amount of comfort for a “Citadin”. 
Naturally, summer and winter travel¬ 


ling are different, and one important 
thing is the footwear, because blisters 
on your toes lead to misery in no time. 
In my summer leather boots, I use two 
pairs of socks and a good felt or leather 
insole. Some people prefer the foam 
rubber insole; I know of two of my 
cruisers who have lost their toes on 
account of wearing rubber boots —- 
rubber makes your feet perspire and 
leads to frozen toes. The only reliable 
footwear for winter travelling in the 
north country and for use on snow- 
shoes is the moose hide or caribou 
moccasin. Three pairs of wollen socks 
and a pair of “Hudson Bay Blanket” 
duffle and a thick felt insole is my wear. 
With that, I get away from the blisters 
and feel comfortable. 

If you have to sleep outdoors without 
any sleeping bag in the winter, make a 
snowhole. Dig right down to the 
ground (with one snowshoe which re¬ 
places a shovel) at the foot of a steep 
incline or small cliff to give you a na¬ 
tural chimney. (Start early, before 
dark. Working with an axe in the 
dark is dangerous.) Insulate the sides 
of the hole and the ground with layers 
of balsam boughs. Cover the hole with 
small three or four-inch poles to form 
some sort of roof. The same Naskaupee 
Indian which I accompanied on some 
caribou hunts used the fresh caribou 
hides for a mattress on top of the 
boughs to sleep on, and more hides, 
flesh side out to cover the roof. 

Chop your dry wood in log lengths, 
five feet long; it takes about one cord 
of wood in twenty-below zero weather 
to keep you comfortable all night in a 
snowhole. Build your fire about four 
feet from the snow hole or shelter, but 
it must be built on the ground. If you 
build it on top of the snow, it will melt 
it to the ground. Do I know it? I tried 

continued on page 181 


178 


Canadian Camping 



One of the unpleasant things Canada 
has to face is the occasional outbreak 
of rabies. These epidemics are not fre¬ 
quent, fortunately, but when they do 
occur they are difficult to control, since 
the disease usually attacks wild ani¬ 
mals, from which it spreads to domestic 
varieties. It is possible to vaccinate 
dogs against rabies and this should be 
done for the safety of the animal and 
the human family, especially dogs in 
rural areas and those taken to the 
country during the vacation periods. 

There is an especially difficult prob¬ 
lem among the borderline pets, that 
can be exceedingly dangerous as car¬ 
riers. Most people who spend their 
summers or vacations in the country 
are thrilled by the small animals from 


stricken by the disease becomes 
changed in personality to the extent 
that he will attack a human or other 
animal. A fox normally keeps well out 
of the way of man but if he becomes 
rabid he is quite likely to rush at and 
attack the creature which normally he 
would cunningly avoid. One of the 
symptoms of danger is abnormal be¬ 
havior of a wild animal. In recent 
cases a fox attacked a man, biting 
through a thick leather boot; a baby 
otter attacked a woman before a mem¬ 
ber of her family shot it; a raccoon bit 
a dog but the latter had, fortunately, 
been vaccinated against the disease. All 
these wild animals were found to be 
rabid. 

There is at present an outbreak cen-

the woods who have developed the art 
of pan-handling to the nth degree. 
Squirrels, raccoons and other wise little 
beasts have learned that the average 
human is a pushover for any show of 
confidence in him by a denizen of the 
wilds. The raccoon has discovered that 
the cheapest way to a good meal is to 
accept it from the paws of the big 
two-legged animals that live in a house. 
The squirrel who has discovered that 
such luxuries as peanuts and walnuts 
are free for the taking, isn’t going to 
wear himself out dashing up and down 
trees, chased by blue jay robbers, when 
he can take all he wishes from a well 
filled hand whose owner is eager and 
dewy-eyed over the favour. 

One rabid animal — a fox, perhaps, 
— can infect every other animal with 
which he comes in contact. The animal 


tering around Eastern Ontario and 
Western Quebec. It would be a good 
idea for the nature lover in these areas 
to go easy on his personal contacts 
with his woodland friends for a while. 
Feed them, if you wish, but make up 
a cafeteria far enough away from your 
actual doors so that you can see them 
but don’t touch them. 

Don’t let your dog or cat run loose 
in the surrounding bush. This is for 
your own protection as well as the 
animal’s. 

Don’t touch or pet any wild animal, 
no matter how tame it may appear to 
be — lack of fear of humans in such 
animals as foxes is a bad sign, remem¬ 
ber. If the animal is one you have 
petted in the past, just remember that 
his main idea has always been food, so

give him his handout but don’t touch 
him or allow him to touch you. You 
may have trouble with the children in 
the family over this, but depending 
upon their age, you will have to make 
them understand that for this summer 
at least, those cute squirrels, ’coons 
and any other members of the woods 
fraternity, may be watched but not 
fed by hand or touched, since they 
may be sick. 

If during your wanderings in the 
bush, you notice an animal that ap¬ 
pears to be sick, or behaves abnormally, 
showing ferociousness where it would 
usually show fear, notify your game- 
warden. If it is necessary for you to 
kill the animal, the head should not 
be damaged. Don’t pick up the body 
of the animal. If it should be necessary 
to transport it from where it is killed, 
make a slip noose of string or rope 
and tie it to a long stick. If you see a 
dead animal in the bush, notify the 
game-warden if it appears to have died 
rather than to have been killed, or 
report it to your nearest Health of 
AnimaLs veterinarian of the Canadian 
Department of Agriculture, which is 
responsible for the control of rabies in 
Canada. 

Rabies may not affect the part of 
the country in which you live or spend 
your summers, but at a time when 
there are reports of outbreaks in speci¬ 
fic places, precautions should be taken 
against any chance of the disease strik¬ 
ing where it could spread to your do¬ 
mestic animals — or family. The 
susceptibility of animals is remarkably 
widespread as to species — cows, small 
rodents, dogs, cats, the larger wild 
beasts such as moose and deer, even 
man himself, may all become infected. 

The disease is not one which imme¬ 
diately shows its symptoms a few hours 
or days after exposure or contact •— 
the incubation period may take from 
one to six months — but once the 
disease is actually diagnosed, death 
may occur in. from two to five days.

In such comfort, civilization for me 
is a thing which does not mean much, 
and with my good friend-hunters I 
have felt like a king away from all of 
this conventional and crazy way of 
living. The only discomfort I had was 
due to the fact that my woollen under¬ 
wear was damp from perspiration. I 
know better now, and I take an extra 
set as a spare, for sleeping purposes, 
which I carry in my lunch bag. Feeling 
dry and warm, even in a snow hole, 
when the frost outside makes the black 
spruce trees crack, is something to 
remember. 

Let us hope that we meet on the 
trail one of these days, you with your 
high powered rifle, and I with my bow 
and arrow. Cheerio, all of you!

QUICK FINISH 
FOR DRIFTWOOD 

Oddly enough, plain, everyday 
common shoe polish is one of the very 
best wood-finishing materials — par¬ 
ticularly for small jobs. Shoe polish is 
easy to manage, provides an excellent 
finish and won’t cause trouble in the 
matter of getting just the right shade. 
(Also, campers can neaten up their 
brogans while they’re at it.) 

Apply polish to the surface, and let 
it dry for an hour or two. Then wipe 
off the excess wax and your finishing 
job is done. (Several coats may be 
necessary to achieve desired darkness; 
apply them the same way.) For very 
important jobs — finishes you want to 
last a long time — shellac and varnish 
may still be the materials you will 
want to use. But of course you don’t 
need to be forewarned about how 
difficult these are to manage.

By A fan Kfeirf 


ONE ASPECT 
OF STAFF SUPERVISION 
IN CAMP 


Not much has been written about 
supervision in camp, although there 
is copious material on staff supervision 
in allied fields. Dr. Hedley Dimock’s 
chapter in “Administration of the 
Modem Camp” is one of the most 
comprehensive statements yet written, 
although he, himelf, indicates the 
need to adapt the techniques of group 
work supervision to the camp situa¬ 
tion. Too few of us have the oppor¬ 
tunity to do that. Many camp people 
feel reluctant to use supervision in 
its fullest sense in camp. This is partly 
due to the fact that the word has 
unfortunate connotations in the mind 
of the average person. 

Many feel that supervision implies 
a formal boss or foreman type relation¬ 
ship. Overseeing or spying, or worse, 
telling the staff member what and how 
to do his job and demanding rigid con¬ 
formance. This is not what is meant. 

Supervision of staff in camp is per¬ 
haps more important than in many 
other fields where it is more readily 
accepted—the average camp today em¬ 
ploys untrained and often young and 
inexperienced staff’. We have rendered 
lip-service to the importance of the 
counsellor in helping camping to reach 
its most honoured objectives. The coun¬ 
sellor is the key person in camp. It is 
he who aids the growth and develop¬ 
ment of the camper. To help those 
counsellors do an effective job is per¬ 


haps the most important single func¬ 
tion of administration. 

Supervision implies that we, with 
greater experience and preparation, 
are responsible for helping the coun¬ 
sellor to develop his abilities to do a 
more effective job, derive satisfaction 
from the job, and develop into a first- 
class staff person. The supervisor is 
responsible to see that a good job is 
done with the campers and also to 
see that his staff is trained to increas¬ 
ingly develop greater skills for the job. 

Many camp directors have privately 
and publicly expressed the idea that 
there is little time in camp for super¬ 
vision. A camp that runs at such a 
tempo or is so understaffed that there 
is no time for staff growth can have 
little time for camper growth. 

The subject of supervision to be ade¬ 
quately treated here would take many 
pages. The only aspects mentioned, 
therefore, will be the how and why 
of staff relations. 

The camp supervisor, i.e., head coun¬ 
sellor, personnel director, program di¬ 
rector, or executive, has as his first big 
job the establishment of good relation¬ 
ships with his staff. He must by word 
and act convince them that he is inter¬ 
ested in helping the counsellor to do a 
good job. He must get across the idea 
that he is not criticizing, not being 
judgemental, but is concerned with the 


182 


Canadian Camping 



campers and staff to bring about the 
objectives of the camp and also for 
everyone to have an enjoyable and 
-worthwhile experience. This implies 
that the supervisor must feel that way. 
He must be able to accept and like 
people, to recognize and give credit to 
the points of view of other staff mem¬ 
bers and to make them feel needed and 
valuable. They are people who will 
discuss problems with staff members, 
permitting and enabling thern to think 
for themselves. That is the key to good 
supervision. 

More often than not, it is the atti¬ 
tudes of the counsellor that are of con¬ 
cern. Perhaps he is too authoritative 
or perhaps we think he is lazy. Both 
are attitudes and must be worked out. 
People do not learn to change by being 
told to or even by having the reason¬ 
ableness and logic of another attitude 
explained to them. Learning can, how¬ 
ever, come through experience and 
sympathetic discussion of the way we 
do things. 

Supervision of staff in camp involves 
certain things that are not technical 
and do not require the skill of a trained 
expert. The first is the establishment 
of a good relationship. This implies 
that the counsellor is made to feel that 
he can discuss problems, present sug¬ 
gestions and count on getting help. 
Regular opportunities for private dis¬ 
cussions with the supervisor are essen¬ 
tial. To say that the supervisor will be 
available if needed is not sufficient, for 
often the person who needs it most is 
the last one to come. If staff are en¬ 
couraged to come regularly, there is 
no feeling that one comes only if there 
are problems, or for a “talking to”. 

The supervisor helps to keep the con¬ 
ference going by asking a few ques¬ 
tions, making a suggestion here and 
there and getting the counsellor to 


either advance a solution, get it off his 
chest, or perhaps get assurance that 
he is doing a good job. Often that 
which is unsaid reveals the counsellor’s 
feelings; and a wise supervisor, by ask¬ 
ing a question or two, can bring to 
light what is beneath the surface. He 
should be a good listener and give only 
such information as is necessary to 
stimulate thinking. He encourages, 
praises, and builds up his staff. He 
looks behind the deed to determine 
the reason for laziness, failure, inabil¬ 
ity to get his group to like him, etc., 
and seeks to get these things discussed. 
He guides the discussion through, 
knowing as much as he cap about his 
counsellor and by having an objective. 
He seeks to enable his staff person to 
do his job. He knows that staff have 
fears, and anxieties about the job, and 
that there must be a chance to release 
these tensions — and above all, he 
knows that a relaxed camp comes from 
relaxed staff. 

I have not said much about tech¬ 
niques, skills in observation, etc. The 
basic skill to be learned is that of de¬ 
veloping our own attitudes. It is easy 
to talk and tell the counsellor what to 
do. It makes us feel good to show that 
we know the answers and can glibly 
rattle off solutions. It is easy to be so 
important, so knowledgable, and so 
ready that we stifle all initiative on 
the part of the staff. It is easy to be 
authoritative and be the administrator 
who hands out policy. Attitudes cannot 
be changed that way and counsellors 
will not reveal to such supervisors the 
problems about which they need the 
most help. We must school ourselves 
to be interested and sympathetic, 
warm and helpful. It is the humility of 
the teacher and his desire to work with 
rather than over or on, that establishes 
a 1 supervisory relationship resulting in 
learning, growth, and above all—good 
camping. 


188 


Toronto , Canada , June 195ft

Canadian Camping 











































FROM THE 
PRESIDENT’S DESK 

By F. M. Van Wagner, President, 
Canadian Camping Association . 


May I say something nice about an 
old and valued friend, the TENT, 
while there is still time? Camping and 
a tent are, for me, so closely associated 
that I cannot think of one without 
including the other. 

Today, we find the tent in need of 
protection, for, no less than some of 
our wild life friends, it is threatened 
with extinction. At the rate it is dis¬ 
appearing from one of its former 
haunts, the summer camp, the next 
generation of campers will have lost 
the thrill and adventure of living in a 
tent. 

Seriously, I should like to say a few 
words in support of tents for general 
camp use. We have in mind a tent, 
overhung by a fly. It must be well 
pitched over an elevated board floor 
and able to withstand any blow short 
of a gale. We also like the fly to over¬ 
hang the tent by 9" to 12" front and 
back, and by 15" to 18" on each side. 
It should have four foot side walls 
that can be rolled up in good weather 
and hooked down to the platform in 
bad weather. There is no more excuse 
for a leaky tent than for a leaky cabin. 
If air and light are wanted, roll the 
walls and you are living out of doors. 


With the walls down, we have full pro¬ 
tection from wind or rain. 

In my opinion, a tent is the ideal 
living quarters for any camper, and I 
believe most campers, if given a choice, 
would take a tent rather than a cabin. 

Why then have cabins so largely re¬ 
placed tents at our summer camps? 
First, there seems to be an opinion 
that a wooden structure is in some way 
superior to a canvas one. A natural 
view, no doubt, for one who has never 
lived in a tent. 

Second, directors prefer cabins be¬ 
cause in the long run they are more 
economical, are easier to maintain, and 
do not have to be put up and taken 
down each season, so, if we are not 
mistaken, the campers’ choice is tents 
while the directors prefer cabins. In 
this contest, the directors are certainly 
winning. The directors’ gain is the 
campers’ loss, and camping, it seems 
to me, has become a little less campy. 

We have expressed our opinion 
about tents, even though the number 
who may agree is diminishing with 
each passing year. What can we do to 
prevent its extinction? 


Toronto, Canada, June 1 ( )oH

THE FOXES OF ONTARIO 



By Dr. C. S. Churcher, 

University of Toronto 3 
Department of Zoology . 

When talking about foxes, most 
people immediately think of the Red- 
fox. Perhaps this is because of our 
familiarity with the European Red-fox 
mentioned in our nursery tales, myths, 
and in Aesop’s fables. However, unlike 
Europe, North America possesses five 
kinds of foxes, of which three are to be 
found in Ontario. These are the Arctic, 
Red, and Gray-foxes of the Arctic 
regions, the coniferous forests, and 
broadleaved forests respectively, and 
the Kit and Desert-foxes of the dry 
southwestern portions of the United 
States. Europe on the other hand, 
possesses only the Red-fox over most 
of its area, with a few Arctic-foxes in 
northern Scandanavia and some 
desert-living foxes in the steppe 
regions of European Russia. 

The most common fox in Ontario is 
the Red-fox, whose scientific name is 
Vulpes vulpes from the Latin word 
‘vulpes’ for a fox. The Red-fox is 
found throughout the temperate 
regions of the northern hemisphere in 
Europe, Asia and North America, and 
his near relatives are found naturally 
in all continents except Australasia. 
This animal is smaller than a dog, 
being about 40 inches in length and 
weighing 12 or 15 lbs. The muzzle is 
fairly long, the ears are pointed, and 
there are a number of long guard-hairs 
scattered throughout his coat. Unlike 
the Arctic-fox, the Red-fox does not 
change his colour with the seasons, 
each individual maintaining the same 
colouration the year round. However, 
individuals vary in colouration quite 
considerably, some being entirely black 


except for a white tip to the tail or 
brush (known as ‘Silver’ in the fur 
trade), some reddish with a dark cross 
on the shoulders (known as ‘Cross’), 
and some more or less red or reddish 
all over (known as ‘Red’). Other 
colour phases are recognized by fur¬ 
riers, but they are less commonly en¬ 
countered in the natural state. In 
general, the average Red-fox has black 
paws and stockings, a white tip to his 
tail, a white throat and underbelly, 
black tips to the ears, and a black 
muzzle, while the rest of the body can 
be of varying shades of black, red, buff, 
or smokey with lighter guard-hairs. 
Individuals with these different colour 
combinations may be found in the 
same litter, just as members of a 
single human family may have differ¬ 
ently coloured hair. 

The Red-fox is found throughout 
the Province of Ontario, and is 
evidently an ancient inhabitant, as its 
presence has been reported from many 
Indian sites by archaeologists. It is one 
of the wild or native animals that seem 
to thrive in the conditions created by 
our agricultural systems, and is now- 
more common in southern Ontario 
than ever before. It prefers roughly 
broken country with a fair amount of 
woodland, grassland, and other forms 
of diverse plant cover. The brakes, 
spinneys, hedgerows, coverts, and 
standing crops make an ideal enviro- 
ment in which he can find his food. 
Each Red-fox has a home territory 
within which it lives and hunts, seldom 
going more than two miles from the 
den. 


186 


Canadian Camping 



The Red-fox lives mainly on mice, 
to which are added frogs, carrion, and 
some small birds, when available, to 
vary the diet. The number of birds, 
especially game birds, which the fox 
will consume is very small, as studies 
of the stomachs of dead foxes have 
shown them to be mainly full of cap¬ 
tured rodents such as rats and mice. It 
is in this role of a mouser and ratter 
that the chief value of the fox lies to 
the farmer. During periods of scarcity 
the Red-fox will eat grasshoppers, 
crickets, maybugs, worms, and fallen 
wild fruit and berries. Especially in 
winter when mice are hard to come by 
will he eat frozen fruit and carrion, 
and even the stray farmyard chicken if 
the farmer does not pen them properly, 
but this fruit and carrion diet is not 
his favourite fare. 

When the Red-foxes pair for breed¬ 
ing, their first problem is to find a 
suitable den. This is frequently the 
discarded burrow of a ground-hog or 
a skunk, which the vixen enlarges to 
suit her needs. This den will be the 
home of the parents, and nursery for 
the next three or four months. The 
den usually has an entrance about ten 
inches in diameter, and may have more 
than one entrance; it is usually situ¬ 
ated on the south side of a slope to get 
the sun. Some dry material such as 
grass or leaves is frequently found 
within the main chamber, acting as 
insulation to keep the young cubs 
warm. Both the dog fox and the vixen 
look after the cubs as they grow 
older, but during the time when the 
vixen is giving birth to the cubs and 
until the cubs are about nine days old, 
and their eyes are open, the dog-fox 
leaves the den to the vixen. The young 
cubs are born in early April or March, 
and number about seven to a litter. 
They live in the den until they are 
about three months old, when they 
leave home to start life on their own, 
usually in June or July. The den is 


therefore mainly a summer home for 
the pair and a refuge for the cubs until 
they can fend for themselves; as soon 
as it is autumn, the cubs depart for ever 
and the parents take to bedding down 
in the thickets and heavy bush, even 
during the coldest weather of winter. 

The least common fox in Ontario 
is the Arctic-fox, whose scientific 
name is Alopex lagopus, from the 
Greek ‘alopex’ a fox and ‘lagopus’ 
meaning rabbit-footed. This animal is 
smaller than either the Red or Gray- 
foxes, being only about 31 inches long 
and weighing on the average about 
eight or ten pounds. The muzzle is 
shorter, the ears are rounded rather 
than pointed, and there is a dense mat 
of hair on the feet to protect the pads 
from the cold of the ice and snow. In 
winter, the usual colour of this fox is 
white, the fur being very dense, soft, 
and long, but in summer the winter 
coat is replaced by a shorter and 
woollier coat of a brownish or bluish- 
gray colour. This change in coloura¬ 
tion for the two main Arctic seasons 
helps the animal to blend more suc¬ 
cessfully into its background, and thus 
to hide it from its enemies such as the 
wolf, and also from its prey such as the 
Arctic hare which cannot see the fox 
creeping upon it. 

The Arctic fox is found in all the 
Arctic lands around the North Pole, 
being known in northern Europe. Asia, 
and North America, as well as from 
Greenland, Iceland, and many of the 
Arctic Is^nds to the north of the 
main landmasses. In Ontario it is re¬ 
stricted to the northern part of the 
province, and only enters it as a visitor 
under the present climatic conditions. 
It has been reported from Fort Severn 
and Cape Henrietta Maria on Hud¬ 
son’s Bay, and from Cochrane and 
Sudbury districts in northern Ontario. 

During the short Arctic summer the 
Arctic-fox lives mainly in open plain 


Toronto , Canada , June 195ft 


187 



or rocky country, feeding off small 
mice, lemmings, birds and their eggs, 
probably any carrion available and 
shell-fish along the sea-shore. In winter 
it takes to the ice, spending as much 
as 90% of its time as far as fifty miles 
from land, and living on the small auks 
or dovekies that are to be found 
amongst the floes. 

During the breeding season, the dog¬ 
fox and the vixen select a burrow in 
the ground as their home, and raise a 
litter of about five cubs. These are born 
any time from May to July, about fifty- 
seven days after mating, and as with 
the Red-fox during this time the dog¬ 
fox absents himself from the den. For 
the next two months both the father 
and mother-fox take care of the cubs, 
but in September the family breaks up 
and the young go their separate ways, 
leaving the parents on the home range. 

Another fox to be found in Ontario 
is the Gray-fox. This is found only 
near the southern borders of Ontario, 
in the Rainy River District, the 
Niagara Peninsula, and between the St. 
Lawrence and Ottawa Rivers. It is 
common in the United States, and 
most of the individuals that are found 
in Canada have probably crossed over 
the Border during winter months when 
the rivers are frozen. 

The Gray-fox differs from the Red- 
fox in having a grizzled gray back and 
top to his head, a blackish tail with a 
black tip, and a generally lighter build. 
Most specimens are about forty inches 
in length and weigh about eight 
pounds. In habits it is very similar to 
the Red-fox, but does differ in two 
interesting particulars. The Gray-fox 
usually makes its den in dense bush, in 
hollow trees, or in cavities in fallen 
rocks, and it lives in these dens 
throughout its life and during the 
whole year, in® contrast to both the 
Arctic and Red-foxes which inhabit 


their dens during the mating and 
breeding seasons only. Another diver¬ 
gent habit of the Gray-fox is in its 
ability to climb trees. It will do this as 
one of its last tricks when pursued by 
hounds or hunters, after having dis¬ 
covered that it can neither outrun nor 
outwit its pursuers. 

In all other habits the Gray-fox is 
similar to the Red-fox, eating approxi¬ 
mately the same diet, having the same 
mating habits, and being as crafty and 
brave as his larger cousin. 

Should anyone wish to seek further 
information on the Ontario foxes, any 
fieldbook of mammals may be of assist¬ 
ance, i.e. “Mammals” by H. S. Zim 
and D. F. Hoffmeister or “A Field 
Guide to the MammaV’ by W. H. 
Burt; or for greater detail, “Mammals 
of North America” by V. H. Gahalane; 
and “Lives of Game Animals”, Volume 
1, by E. T. Seton, may be consulted. 
These latter two references contain a 
wealth of detail covering all aspects of 
the life of these mammals, and are very 
readable in every way. 

As a confirmation of the traditional 
wisdom of the Red-fox, the following 
story has been told to me: A Red-fox 
had his den near a farm house, and 
was often seen by the farmer as it 
caught small rodents in his fields. All 
the neighbouring farms were frequent¬ 
ly robbed of their fowls and ducks by 
foxes, but none of the foxes was ever 
caught. At long last one such animal 
was caught robbing a hen house, and 
the culprit shot. After that night, the 
depredations on the other farms 
ceased, but also the fox that was often 
seen by the first farmer was never seen 
again. It is logical to conclude that the 
culprit was the same animal, which, in 
its wisdom, did not rob the nearest 
farm for fear of stirring up trouble in 
what was his home sanctuary.

Sermons Unber je 


One of our active and prolific writers 
for Canadian Camping , Mr. Ed. Devitt, 
of Camp Comak, has kindly sent us the 
following story, “May I Help? 93 “If it 
will assist any other directors or coun¬ 
sellors in their search for a sermon 
topic 99 he writes f “1 hope they will feel 
free to use it. 99 


Offering to help is the “Open 
Sesame” to accomplishment, satisfac¬ 
tion, comradeship and happiness at 
camp and everywhere. It is a magic 
key that not all campers understand 
and use. In fact, campers can be 
classified in three groups according to 
this principle. 

This first group includes the unfor¬ 
tunate few^who never offer to help. 
But it r is unfortunate, too, that this 
group seems 1 tb be increasing in num¬ 
ber. It. would appear that more and 
more- hoys^and_girls take it for granted 
that more and more things will be 
done for them in the natural course of 
events. These things include such items 
as preparing meals, waiting on table, 
washing dishes, to take a few examples 
from the camp situation. It is amazing 
how many otherwise kind, considerate, 
thoughtful and unselfish campers will 
simply sit down at table and expect to 
be waited on without ever thinking 
that they might have a responsibility 
for offering to help. Most would help 
if they thought of it but the thought 
noes not occur to them. There are 
others who consciously or uncon¬ 
sciously keep the thought out of their 
minds and others who refrain from 
acting if the thought does come. 

The second group includes the many 
who will help when asked. Many of 
these feel a genuine regret that they 
did not think of offering to help. Most 
will respond willingly enough for at 
least a short period. But how far do 


S>un ... 

we fall short in our helpfulness when 
we stop soon after we start, for some 
personal, selfish reason or because the 
work and effort involved is too strenu¬ 
ous? True helpfulness frequently 
demands physical and mental strain, 
sustained effort after we would like to 
stop, sacrifice of personal wishes and 
desires, sometimes for a long period of 
time. The true helper sees the whole 
job through, no matter what the cost. 

This leads to the third group, the 
choice few, the real campers who spon¬ 
taneously offer to help whenever the 
opportunity arises. They are always 
willing. Unfortunately in spite of their 
willingness, some of these do not have 
the talent and ability to translate their 
desire to help in sustained, creative 
helpfulness, but the spirit is there. How 
that spirit is appreciated! 

This leads to the choicest of the 
choice: the select few who combine 
with their genuine desire to help, the 
capacity to figure things out for them¬ 
selves; and who, even in the process 
of helping, think through the next 
step, and anticipate the next move 
without having to be told. They are 
blessed with a functioning, practical 
intelligence along with a true desire to 
help. This makes their helpfulness 
that much more valuable. 

One of the notable queries in the 
English language is a sincere, genuine 
“May I Help?” It sets people'apart. It 
raises them to the plane of a true 
Christian, of a real camper. It means 
that we instinctively admire and like 
them, for they are the people who get 
things done, who realize the joy and 
satisfaction of accomplishment, who* 
win and earn friends, who enjoy true 
happiness. Let us hope that our offer¬ 
ing to help, at any time, may be an 
Open Sesame for all of us. 

—•

(d) Do the campers want to go out 
on another trip soon? — with 
you? 

(e) Is the equipment you received 
fit to go out again immedi¬

2. Are you planning to go over the 
trip with your campers the very 
night of your return? 

3. Gan each boy list two or three 
positive additions to his knowledge, 
some new skills mastered, in addi¬ 
tion to toughened muscles? 

4. Are you ready to take out another 
trip tomorrow? 

Well, as you can see, the list is 
endless. No doubt you have thought 
of at least a dozen additions. If you 
have, this list has accomplished its 
purpose at least in part, of making you 
think. Common sense after all, is the 
essence of good camping. 

Bon voyage!

NATURE STUDY 

A good way to help familiarize the 
camper with the camp surroundings, is 
to label the trees and flowers in the 
area. The use of 3” x 5” index cards 
and some tacks or tape should do the 
trick, and make the camp area better 
known to each camper. Labelling the 


area can also be an educational pro¬ 
ject for the campers, and can be made 
into an interesting outdoor game. Div¬ 
ide the campers into even groups. 
Here you can easily mix the groups, 
so that older and younger boys or girls 
will work together. Assign each group 
to an area around the camp. The 
group that correctly identifies the most 
trees and flowers with the appropriate 
index cards is the winner.

QUEBEC 

A highly successful camping confer¬ 
ence was held jointly by the Canadian 
Camping Association and the Quebec 
Camping Association in Montreal, at 
the Windsor Hotel, on April 11th and 
12th, 1958. Highlights included such 
speakers as Paul Provencher, Dr. F. 
A. Urquhart, Prof. Reynold Carlson, 
Mr. Charles Stafford, Mr. Robson 
Black, and many others. 

When the Programme Committee of 
the Quebec and Canadian Camping 
Conference were struggling with the 
content for programme, it was sug¬ 
gested the French Camps should have 
some opportunity to participate. The 
Committee insisted nothing should be 
planned for them without their consent 
and co-operation. The Chairman, Nan 
Vail, and Tony Shorgan, undertook 
the task and the latter called a meet¬ 
ing of the French directors. 

Some fifteen persons attended and 
under the chairmanship of Mr. Rene 
St. Onge, discussed the possibilities. 
They became interested, not only in 
the Conference, but in organizing a 
French section. Much work followed 
on the part of these two gentlemen 
and as a result, two sessions were 
organized, one on Saturday morning 
to discuss the possibility of forming a 
French section, the other an afternoon 


session when Rev. Father Dube, c.s.c., 
director Camp l’Escale, spoke on “L’es- 
prit qui doit regner dans un de 
vacances”. 

The groups also assisted the Con¬ 
ference Committee by helping secure 
booths and generally added to the 
success of the venture. 

At the morning, Saturday, April 
11th session, after considerable discus¬ 
sion, following a brief presentation by 
F. M. Van Wagner, President of the 
Canadian Camping Association, a very 
wise conclusion was reached. A Com¬ 
mittee of five was named to work with 
the group for one year, holding meet¬ 
ings, planning, finding out what such 
an organization could accomplish and 
how much support they could expect. 
In other words, slow, careful work was 
to be undertaken. 

Previous to the afternoon session, the 
Committee met, and Tony Shorgan 
was chosen as Chairman. He stated 
that with the necessary support, his 
Committee would bend their efforts 
toward developing interest, plan meet¬ 
ings, carry out consultation with the 
Q.C.A. Executive, and plan for the 
future. 

We are all confident that what seems 
like a modest beginnining may develop 
into, something very worth while for 
Canadian Camping.

NOVA SCOTIA 

In a downtown office in Halifax in 
March, 1955, the idea* of a camp con¬ 
ference workshop was tossed around 
amongst five people keenly concerned 
with the development of camping in 
Nova Scotia. This idea was just the 
beginning of a pooling of interests and 
enthusiasm of camp-minded indivi¬ 
duals towards better camps in the 
province by the sea. 

At this meeting, before programme 
was discussed, several prerequisites 
were laid down: firstly, the location 
must be a campsite; it should be cen¬ 
trally located in the province; the pro¬ 
gramme should be basic; the natural 
resources of the site should be used to 
the fullest possible extent; the cost 
should be kept at a minimum; the time 
should be such that leaders, who are 
also teachers, students, doctors, clergy¬ 
men, business men and women, could 
attend. With a strong committee in 
action, plans for the first Leaders 
Workshop for the province began to 
materialize. 

The site was ideal -— an island in a 
lake near Waverly. The Adirondack 
cabins which house Wolf Cubs during 
a regular camp session, accommodated 
the thirty-three representatives of wel¬ 
fare, church, Y,M. and Y.W.C.A., 
Scout and Girl Guide camps. A patrol 
of scouts set up a camp unit near the 
main camp to demonstrate pioneer 
camping. 

A nutritionist of the Department of 
Public Health had planned the menus 
and arranged the ordering with a view 
to keeping costs to a minimum. A new 
camp cook was broken in that week¬ 
end and found his new camp family 
most appreciative. 

Various agencies and government 
departments got behind the scheme. 


Contacts were made and notices circu¬ 
lated by the Physical Fitness Branch of 
the Department of Education. The 
Museum of Natural Science had 
scouted out the area in advance and 
the geologist had prepared maps and 
diagrams of the geological formations. 
An expert naturalist led a field trip 
which introduced the group to other 
inhabitants of the island, a pair of 
cedar waxwings, the beavers’ handi¬ 
work, an ant colony which sprang into 
immediate action at the rude advances 
of the visitors. 

Late in the afternoon, half-kneeling 
forms could be seen bent over unsus¬ 
pecting victims in a practice of the 
Holger Nielsen method of Artificial 
Respiration under the guidance of the 
Red Cross Swimming and Water Safe¬ 
ty Director. 

At the firelight programme on Sat¬ 
urday night, the Saga of the Disap¬ 
pearing Moose was portrayed in vivid 
realism. A Fire Dance and shadow- 
craft were also delightful entertain¬ 
ment, from both the participant and 
the spectator’s point of view. Assis¬ 
tance was given here by the Assistant 
Dramatics Adviser of the Department 
of Education. 

A swap session of real “know how” 
gave programme and administration 
ideas — a survival kit by a scouter, 
plaster crafts from the dentist, dish 
washing schemes, to name a few. 

It was soon discovered — not a 1 sur¬ 
prising fact, but a reassuring one — 
that problems which each had experi¬ 
enced were not peculiar to him alone 
but were shared by all camp people 
alike. What happens when the weather¬ 
man provides day after day of rainy 
weather? How can the counsellor help 
the homesick camper? How long will 
camps be able to obtain volunteer 


Toronto, Canada , June 1958 


193 



leaders, and then what will the answer 
be? 

A unity and oneness of purpose and 
interests soon became felt among these 
leaders. This feeling was soon trans¬ 
ferred into action when an impromptu 
business meeting was called on the 
spot. There followed a motion that 
a meeting be called in September to 
consider the formation of a Camping 
Association. 

On September 26, representatives 
named at the workshop in June held 
the Inaugural Meeting of the Nova 
Scotia Camping Association. By Nov¬ 
ember 28, the constitution was adopted. 

Since then the Association has 
grown slowly but surely. Annual spring 
conferences have been held in conjunc¬ 
tion with the annual meetings. The 
theme of the first conference was “Pre- 
Camp Planning”, a much-needed con¬ 
cept for all camps. The next year, the 
programme was woven around leader¬ 
ship. 

Another major milestone in its young 
life was the adoption of the Nova 
Scotia fledgling into the Canadian 
Camping Association family. For the 
first time, this eastern Association was 
officially represented at the Annual 
Conference held recently in Montreal. 

Now an annual institution, the 
Camp Leaders’ Workshop has moved 
around to various campsites. In 1956 
it was held at Camp Kadimah, the 
Jewish Community Camp on Lake 
William. The site in 1957 was Rain¬ 
bow .Haven, the camp for less fortunate 
children in Halifax, located on a 
sand beach of a bay off the Atlantic. 

This year on May 9 to 11, Big Cove 
Y.M.C.A^ Camp will play host to the 
third annual workshop of the Nova 
Scotia Camping Association. 


EASTERN ONTARIO 

“How do you do four men’s jobs at 
once?” was a question asked of Mr. 
“Bill” White when, after five minutes, 
he made a group of 150 untrained 
voices into a choir. The 150 were the 
persons who attended the Eastern 
Ontario Camping Association Confer¬ 
ence, and “Bill” had just finished a 
discussion and demonstration on 
“Music in Camp.” 

The Conference was held in 
Ottawa on May 9th and 10th with a 
programme based on the varied aspects 
of camping. Sessions included “Health 
and Safety”, “Tests and Awards”, “To 
Have or Not To Have”, “Parents and 
Camp” and “Staff Relationships” for 
Administrations, and “Waterfront 
Special Events”, Counsellor Responsi¬ 
bilities”, “Dramatics” and “Out Trips 
and Hikes” for Counsellors. For those 
interested in Camp Programme, the 
topics were “Approaches to Program¬ 
ming”, “Special Events”, “Program¬ 
ming by Age Group” and “Evening 
Events”. 

The Friday evening session took the 
form of a “Fighting Words” panel on 
controversial quotations about camp¬ 
ing. No questions were answered but 
the panel members, made up of 
specialists in recreation, sociology and 
camping, provided much food for 
though t. 

Special visitors who helped with the 
Conference programme included—Mr. 
Fred Van Wagner, President C.C.A.; 
Miss Agnes Mutchler, President 
Q.C.A.; Mrs. Eanswythe Flynn, Execu¬ 
tive Secretary O.C.A.; Miss Nan Vail, 
Past-President C.C.A.; and Mr. Bill 
White.

Canadian Camping 




HAVE YOU TRIED 
ORIENTEERING? 


By Bill Salo , 

Secretary , Orienteering Services . 


For those who have tried Orienteer¬ 
ing or are using it extensively, the term 
will be familiar. Simply ... it is a 
term based on the Scandinavian word 
“Orientering” . . . meaning to orient 
oneself to one’s surroundings. To adapt 
the word for use in English, the addi¬ 
tion of one letter “e”, gave to it the 
same outdoor flavour as “mountaineer¬ 
ing”, “pioneering” and other related 
terms. To sum it up, Orienteering is a 
broad, outdoors programme of games, 
exercises and personal experiences in 
forest travel, revolving from small to 
large circles around the ability to use 
maps and compasses effectively. 

Basically, the word does not truly 
picture the range or scope of the 
activity. As thought of in Sweden, 
where Orienteering was put into seri¬ 
ous use some 40 years ago, it is a 
competitive sport; cross-country racing 
on foot using a map and compass to 
determine and follow the best routes. 
The highly developed methods used 
there have grown with the years, and 
it would be somewhat premature to 
envision Orienteering in camps in 
Canada on such a specialized plane; 
and it is not necessary to do so. Orien¬ 
teering is very flexible. 


This very feature of flexibility is, 
perhaps, one of the strongest features 
of this activity in assessing it for the 
Canadian Camp programme. Without 
fear of losing any of its effectiveness 
as a strongly inspirational, cleverly 
educational and physically invigorating 
sport, the camp director can adjust his 
plans for Orienteering to suit the needs 
and fulfill the desires of the instructing 
personnel and those whom they coun¬ 
sel. In combination with other usual 
camp activities such as canoeing, 
hiking, nature trail tramping and over¬ 
night tripping, Orienteering can pro¬ 
vide that extra taste of adventure for 
all concerned. Youngsters like to think 
of themselves as Indians, pioneers or 
famous coureur-de-bois, challenging the 
wilderness of the forest. Orienteering 
can stimulate the imagination to that 
extent and beyond. 

How to Introduce it 

Once the What and Why of a ques¬ 
tion has been answered, it is logical to 
enquire into the How. In this respect, 
it will interest every camp director to 
know that the introduction of Orien¬ 
teering to the camp programme is a 
simple matter. One primary requisite 


Toronto, Canada, June 1958 


199 



is, of course, a qualified instructor on 
the staff. At this time, the amount and 
scope of material available for such 
instructors is quite adequate to give 
anyone the necessary qualifications 
after study and some application. 

Aids and Material 

There is one primary source of 
material and information on Orien¬ 
teering in Canada. This is The Can¬ 
adian Orienteering Service, 77 York 
Street, Toronto, Ontario. They have 
and will supply the materials for in¬ 
structors and camps, some of which 
are listed in this article. 

The basic Orienteering Handbook is 
called “Be Expert With Map and Com¬ 
pass”. This is the chief authority on 
the sport. By Bjorn Kjellstrom, a noted 
Swedish Champion Orienteerer, this 
book of 136 pages is written and illus¬ 
trated in a basic, non-technical man¬ 
ner. It contains many ideas on games 
and exercises which can be put into 
immediate use, generally revolving 
around the concept of finding direc¬ 
tion, and travelling on bearings from 
maps, using a magnetic compass. This 
book is recommended reading for any 
Orienteering instructor and it will be¬ 
come his helpmate in many ways. At¬ 
tached to the back cover of the book 
is an envelope containing postcards 
which can be mailed for other material 
and for the map index sheets, as well 
as a practicing compass and protractor. 

Three basic tools for the instructor 
in addition to the above mentioned 
book are a Pathfinder map for setting 
up an Orienteering Area in the camp 
surroundings, an Instructor’s Portfolio, 
and a set of the Compass Game. The 
Orienteering Area map is a specially 
drawn chart showing how eight 
separate activities using a map and 
compass can be organized within a 
very limited area, and this chart is 


complete with instructions on each of 
the eight different parts. The Instruc¬ 
tor’s Portfolio is designed to provide a 
plan of action, and covers both the 
theoretical and the practical aspects of 
the sport. The Compass Game consists 
of 20 separate contestants’ cards and 
a master card containing instructions 
for setting up the game with the cor¬ 
rect answers. 

To add extra spice to the Orienteer¬ 
ing sessions in camp, there are two 16 
mm. sound-colour films available for 
purchase or for rental. A limited num¬ 
ber of prints of both “MAP AND 
COMPASS” and “THE SPORT OF 
ORIENTEERING” are in circulation 
on a free distribution basis for single 
showings and can be obtained, if not 
booked solid, upon application to the 
Canadian Orienteering Service. Trans¬ 
portation costs in both directions are 
the only charges made. 

TOPOGRAPHIC MAPS 

Maps of the area surrounding each 
camp are a prime requisite. The best 
ones are National Topographic series, 
in the scale, if possible, of 1 mile to J 
inch. Not all areas are mapped as yet 
in this scale, and it may be necessary 
to use some native ingenuity to obtain 
the most suitable maps. Aerial photo¬ 
graphs are usually available in areas 
which are not mapped and they can 
be used very effectively for making 
your own. County survey maps are 
also useful where no topographies are 
as yet available. 

Sources of supply for topographic 
maps are the Map Distribution Branch, 
Department of Mines and Technical 
Surveys, Ottawa; your Provincial De¬ 
partment of Lands and Forests or its 
equivalent, and some stationery and 
book stores. 


200 


Canadian Camping 



Compasses 

Orienteering, even in its very junior 
stages, requires a protractor compass 
of a special kind. This magnetic com¬ 
pass combines the features of a pro¬ 
tractor and compass mounted on a 
transparent plastic plate. This feature 
makes these instruments unbeatable 
when working map and compass to¬ 
gether. Information on sources of 
supply may be obtained by mailing in 
the right card provided in the Orien¬ 
teering Handbook for this purpose. 

How Much? 

The cost of setting up an Orienteer¬ 
ing programme in camp is one of the 
strong features in its favour. The initial 
expenses are low, and any recurring 
costs are directly related to the scope 
and intensification of a developing 
programme. It is normal to start on a 
modest scale, expanding activities and 
equipment gradually. In this way, it 
is possible to avoid the heavy strain 
on resources which many other out¬ 
doors activities sometimes entail. Ten 
to twenty people at a time can be 
active, with equipment costing no more 
than about fifty dollars. In camps 
where some of the equipment is avail¬ 
able for purchase by the youngsters 
themselves, the capacity can be 
doubled or tripled at the same cost. 

It is expected that much serious 
consideration is being given to a wider 
use of this new activity during the 
coming seasons. Based on the experi¬ 
ence which many will acquire, it will 
be interesting to see how well the fun¬ 
damentals are accepted by the final 
court of opinion . . . the youngsters 
themselves.
