WILL THESE INTEREST YOUR CAMPERS? 

By G. C. Toner, 



Always there is room in the camp 
programme, perhaps around the camp¬ 
fire, or at the dinner table, for reliable 
information about the flora and fauna 
of the rural area about us. Mr. Toner 
has been writing for some years on 
just such topics, many of which have 
appeared in the Bancroft Times. Can¬ 
adian Camping has been given permis¬ 
sion to reprint a collection of his tid¬ 
bits, for their extreme value to the 
camp directors and staff members . . . 
all of us who sometimes find it difficult 
to put our fingers on this kind of infor¬ 
mation. Why not clip these stories and 
paste them in that looseleaf memo 
book we should be preparing now for 
summer use? 

BASS 

It would be impossible to estimate 
the number of black bass there are 
in Ontario lakes and streams, for 
they are distributed throghout the 
province from the Quebec to the 
Manitoba boundaries and northward 
to beyond Lake Nipissing. Though 
heavily fished, stocking by the 
Department of Lands and Forests, 
moving over-populous fish from one 
lake to another in which there is 
plenty of food, but not enough fish, 
and, other conservation measures, 
bass fishing is as good now as it 
has ever been — even better than 
some years in the past. 


The fish take readily to transfer. 
Time was when bass could not be 
found in such large bodies of water 
as the Lake of the Woods; today, it 
is one of the most popular fish in 
that area. Mike Ament, once 
operator of a fishing camp on Little 
Vermillion Lake near Hudson, put 134 
adult bass into the lake twenty years 
ago. - Today, it is claimed, although 
it may be a slight exaggeration, bass 
are ,so thick you need a plough on 
both ends, of the boat to get through 
the water. 

The story is somewhat similar in 
southeastern Ontario regions where 
many camp operators and individuals 
complained some lakes had too many 
small bass. There were so many fish 
in some lakes that the water could 
not support them in food. 

Some complainers asked that the 
lakes be stocked with larger fish— 
but that wasn’t the solution. Study 
carried out by the Fish and Wildlife 
Division of the Department indicated 
there were already too many fish, and 
netting was carried out with the small 
fish being removed to other bodies of 
water which could support them. The 
result was successful; bass in the 
original lake grew larger and those 
transferred found more food and better 
living conditions. 


202 


Canadian Camping 








It is likely the two types of bass 
run about even in numbers. In the 
warmer waters of southern Ontario, 
particularly in the Rideau chain and 
parts of Haliburton, the large-mouth 
variety predominate. In colder waters, 
the small-mouth takes over. As a rule, 
the large-mouth grows bigger, with 
average weight varying from two to 
three pounds, while the small-mouth 
may average between I /2 and 2 l A 
pounds. However, there are bigger bass 
caught each year. The world’s record 
large-mouth weighed more than 22 
pounds and was caught in the warm 
waters of Georgia. It is not unusual 
for a seven or eight-pounder to be 
taken in Ontario. The world’s record 
small-mouth bass was taken in Florida 
and weighed 14 pounds. In 1951, a 
similar fish weighing nine pounds two 
ounces was caught in Macauley Lake 
in Nipissing County and this fish is 
believed to be the largest of its kind 
ever caught in Canada. 

What makes the bass such a favour¬ 
ite? First of all, of course, is his superb 
fighting qualities. He jumps, dives, 
circles and battles to the fcast gasp. 
There are times, of course, when he 
refuses to do anything. 

Every fisherman has experienced 
times when bass could be seen swim¬ 
ming lazily about in fairly shallow 
water and so thick they resembled a 
living carpet of fish. Yet the fish have 
refused to strike at anything offered. 
About the time bass fishing seems to 
be completely futile, the fish may begin 
to strike. When they do, there probably 
isn’t a more enthusiastic fish to be 
found. 

Favourite food of the large-mouth 
is fish, crayfish, frogs, insects, but 
they’ll tackle almost any kind of arti¬ 
ficial lures from plugs to light spinning

LOG DRIVES 

At one time there was a big log 
drive every spring on the York river. 
Those were the days when the b:g 
pine still flourished in this region, be¬ 
fore there were automobiles and trucks 
to take the logs to the mills. River and 
railroad were the only ways the logs 
could be hauled. Railroad haulage was 
expensive but the river drive with its 
high water in the spring was not too 
costly and this was the way the major¬ 
ity of the timber went to the mills. 
Those days are past as far as the York 
is concerned, but river driving still 
occurs each spring. 

There’s a sense of urgency, an 
atmosphere of expectancy along the 
ice-filled rivers of Northern Ontario as 
the fabulous river-drivers await the 
moment the logs begin to move. Spring 
drives are almost ready to start and 
one of Canada’s most spectacular jobs 
about to begin. 

True it is that trucks, tractors, rail¬ 
ways have been carrying logs from the 
pulpwood and lumber camps through¬ 
out the winter. But millions of board 
feet of logs have been piled on the 
ice of lakes or on the river banks ready 
for the roaring waters to move them 
toward the mill-ponds. 

To keep them moving are the 
drivers, some of them youngsters barely 
out of their teens, others veterans of a 
score of drives, many still celebrated 
in song and fireside legend throughout 
Northern Ontario. 


204 


Canadian Camping 







There’s hardly a major river in the 
north which doesn’t have a log drive. 
The Upper Ottawa, the Mississauga, 
the Marten, the Pic, Nipigon, the 
Aguasabon, all boat their valuable car¬ 
goes to lakes on which mills are situ¬ 
ated. Here the logs are boomed, held 
for storage, pulled up the jackladders 
into the mills to be sawn into lumber 
or crushed, beaten “dissolved” for 
manufacture of a thousand varieties of 
paper. 

The rush to meet a newspaper dead¬ 
line isn’t any greater than is the hurry 
to move a log cut. Timing has to be 
just perfect; the moment the ice melts 
or goes out of lake or river, logs which 
have been either piled on the lake ice 
or along the banks of the river begin 
to move. They must be kept moving, 
for only during the spring run-off, the 
high water, can they be kept afloat. 


Hang-ups — in which logs are 
stranded Qn shoals, are not only un¬ 
economical, but also call for tremend¬ 
ously heavy works. Log jams can be 
averted — sometimes — by careful 
“feeding” of the river. But despite man¬ 
made plans, they still happen and, in 
cases, they can hold up an entire drive. 
Hence the immediate call for skilled 
jam-breakers, men who can walk a 
rolling log as delicately and quickly as 
a cat, who can throw a cable loop 
around a key log with utmost skill or 
place a bundle of dynamite sticks in a 
strategic spot without turning a hair. 

Despite advances in equipment and 
technique, there still hasn’t been much 
change in the equipment used on the 
log drive. The load has been lessened 
to some extent by the use of aluminum 
for pike poles, the use of tractors 
instead of horses. But the drive still

needs strong, skilled men who can wade 
in icy waters all day, work in wet 
clothes from morning till night and can 
tell at a glance which logs are holding 
up the drive. 

Top river drivers can glance at a 
river — even a strange river — and 
detect unfailingly just how booms 
should be placed to divert logs around 
obstacles, into favourable eddy or back¬ 
water; how long a drive should take, 
almost to the minute, including the 
cleaning up process which sees the 
drivers with iheir peavies and pikes 
moving stranded logs into faster and 
deeper waters. 

Some of them have never worked on 
any other river; some have worked 
every one from the Ottawa to Lake 
of the Woods. They work hard and 


they play hard — although there have 
been many changes since the old days 
of $30-a-month-and-found — for the 
skilled river driver of today is one of 
the highest paid men in the bush. 

There are few tougher grinds than 
a major log drive. Food is served, in 
many cases, from a floating kitchen 
which accompanies the drives. In 
times of emergency the men may not 
even take time to eat for its is essen¬ 
tial the logs be kept moving before the 
water subsides — which may be over¬ 
night on some rivers. 

Soon the northern rivers will be full 
of logs, the drives will be over and the 
drivers again, as they have done for 
many years, will celebrate the comple¬ 
tion of the winter harvest of timber 
from Ontario’s forests.

STONE PITS of LAKE SUPERIOR 

Were the stone pits of Lake Superior 
built “to combat the Sioux Indians 
when they were on their massacre 
tours?” Or were the stone depressions 
found during the past few years along 
the Superior coast dynamite storage 
pits dating back to the construction of 
the Canadian Pacific Railway? 

How far do they extend to the east 
from the Bering Straits where once the 
Mongolian peoples crossed to North 
America? 

These are questions now being stud¬ 
ied by rangers, conservation officers 
and foresters of the Ontario Depart¬ 
ment of Lands and Forests who are 
reporting discovery of new pits in 
Northern Ontario. 

Originally, the pits — elliptical de¬ 
pressions of about nine by eleven feet 
on raised beaches of the lake — were 


discovered by Colin MacMillan of 
Marathon and investigated subse¬ 
quently by experts from the University 
of Toronto and Royal Ontario Mus¬ 
eum. The Lands and Forests Depart¬ 
ment was supplied with photographs 
and material about the pits and asked 
to join in the search for others which 
may establish that the Mongolian 
peoples, according to the experts, 
travelled into Eastern Canada between 
8,000 and 10,000 years ago — and 
possibly longer. 

Since June 1957, when officials of 
Marathon Corporation, the University 
and the Museum made the first inten¬ 
sive search of the Lake Superior shore 
for the pits and found nearly 200, 
Lands and Forests pilots and rangers 
have been photographing the area and 
searching for more. 

The only logical explanation for the 
pits, it is believed, is that they were

by the nomads from Asia and were 
built by the Mongols who overturned

Lands and Forests men report a 
pit on north Limestone Island west of 
Parry Sound. “It has evidently been 
there for a considerable period, as 
judged by the moss growing on the 
stones. There are some stories relating 
to Indian battles fought at the Lime¬ 
stone Islands.” the Department 

reports. 

Meanwhile, another has been repor¬ 
ted some distance up a river in the 
Pays Plat area. (Most of the ones 
discovered to date have been on the 
shore — the raised beaches — of Lake 
Superior.) In the Pays Plat area local 
Indians say this one and another near¬ 
by were built to repel the Sioux. Still 
another has been found on Pie Island 
in Lake Superior while another north¬ 
east of Redditt is now under investiga¬ 
tion. 

A much larger pit found in the jack- 
fish area is believed to have been a 
dynamite cache used by railways 
workers during the construction of 
the C.P.R. 

Discovery of the original pits 
aroused wide scientific interest. Details 
and photographs were sent to 
scientists in all parts of the world by 
Dr. J. Norman Emmerson and Prof. T. 
F. Mcllwraith of the University of 
Toronto and by Dr. V. B. Meen of 
the Royal Ontario Museum. So far, 
however, they believe there is nothing 
exactly resembling the stone structures 
in other parts of the world.

continued from page 169 

promised in the brochure you are 
reading, perhaps for the first time. 

Quite naturally, you will be guided 
in your ultimate choice by the section 
of the country in which the camp 
being considered is located. Has it a 
particular fee within your capacity to 
pay? Does it meet the other personal 
requirements which only you can de¬ 
cide are important? It should be ob¬ 
vious that the best course to take 
would be to give consideration to more 
than one camp; and when you have 
done so, get an outside appraisal from 
other parents whose children have 
attended. 

A personal visit to the camp site is 
advisable when the camp is in opera¬ 
tion. However, this is not always pos¬ 
sible or practical. The suggestion is 
made on the assumption that care is 
taken by the parent in making the 
choice and that the visit might well 
take place a year before your child 
will go to camp. 

One last very important considera¬ 
tion: the boy or girl camper should 
be in on the final decision and this 
should mean that the potential camper 
might well be on hand when you go 
to meet the camp directors, to see the 
camp site, to watch other campers on 
location. A new camper should go 
to camp willingly because his interest 
has been aroused and not because he 
is “sent” — or should it be said, “sen¬ 
tenced” ? 

Parents can help raise the standards 
of camping. By evaluating the camp 
experiences of their boy or girl, 
parents can make constructive sugges¬ 
tions to camp committees and to camp 
directors. The parent has not shelved 
his responsibility by finally choosing a 
camp for his child. As with the school, 
the parent should cooperate with all 
concerned to achieve the greatest bene¬ 
fit for the camper who is his child.

It was with this thought in mind that the new ACA song book 
was developed. Thousands of camping people responded to ques¬ 
tionnaires which the compiling committee used in developing the 
new book. 

The book is functional and practical. Between its covers are 
the old favourites of camping groups plus new songs which it is 



anticipated, will soon become fav¬ 
ourites. The inexperienced coun¬ 
selor can find songs which are 
easily sung. There is an excellent 
selection of an inspiring variety 
of the best beloved songs for tra¬ 
ditional occasions and the most 
meaningful for special occasions. 

Response has been most en¬ 
thusiastic. Copies can be obtained 
from the American Camping 
Association, Martinsville, Indiana. 
Prices: 1 to 24 copies, 35 c each; 
25-49 copies, 30c each; 50 or 
more copies, 25c each.
